choices.feedback: The office calls within three days to schedule. A formal letter with a deadline isn't aggression here — it's the recognized grammar of a dispute, and it tells the firm you know the procedure they are legally bound by, which re-sorts you out of the 'can wait' pile.

choices.text: You keep calling the office in a friendly tone, empathize with their busy season, and avoid words like Frist or Haftung so as not to poison the relationship.
choices.feedback: September becomes October. In a contract culture, goodwill without a written Frist creates little to answer to — legally or socially — and friendly patience tends to be read, accurately, as someone who can be deprioritized.

choices.text: You get the Meister himself on the phone and go hard: lawyer threats, one-star reviews, and a few words about what kind of outfit he runs.
choices.feedback: He stops taking your calls and refers you back to the office. Hard conflict itself is normal in this assertive culture — but Sachlichkeit demands you attack the defect, not the man, and threats issued before any Frist was even set read as bluster rather than strength.

choices.text: You take charge of the whole mess: coordinate the neighbor, the Hausverwaltung, and the firm's Betriebshaftpflicht insurer, then propose one joint on-site Termin with a written agenda.
choices.feedback: Everyone accepts, because someone competent finally owns the problem. Authority is granted readily here when it arrives as organization plus documentation rather than as rank or volume — you have made yourself the person the file goes through.

caveats: Hofstede's German scores are effectively West German scores; three decades after reunification, East-West differences in institutional trust, income, and social norms persist, and Leipzig or Rostock will diverge from what these averages describe.

Berlin — especially its international startup and creative scenes — runs looser norms than Munich or Swabia; an English-speaking Berlin workplace may actively penalize some advice in this pack, while a Bavarian small town is more formal than our big-city default. Sie/du conventions and punctuality are also visibly loosening among under-35s.

Hofstede's core data comes from IBM employee surveys run 1967-1973; the LTO score (83) comes from a later, different instrument and is among the most contested figures for Germany. Treat all six numbers as coarse priors, not measurements of anyone you will meet.

In Germany's big cities the share of residents with a migration background runs from roughly a third (Berlin) to over half (Frankfurt); Turkish-German, post-Soviet, and other communities operate partly distinct norm sets that this pack's socialDelta values do not model.

socialDelta scores mainstream approval of visible behavior — not moral worth, and not what's psychologically good for you. Within-country individual variation dwarfs the differences between country averages.

voiceNotes.archetypist: Germany is what a society looks like when it answers chaos with order and then writes the order down. Look at the structure: power distance of 35 next to uncertainty avoidance of 65 — the hierarchy is flat, but the procedure is iron. You cannot perform status here; you have to demonstrate competence, and the system will audit you if you try to skip that step. The craftsman and sage strategies pay because responsibility in this culture means the boring kind — documentation, deadlines, showing up sorted, doing your stairwell week. If you want to be the sovereign, understand that authority is downstream of demonstrated competence: earn the right to impose order by first submitting to it, visibly, for longer than feels fair.
voiceNotes.clinician: If you're temperamentally an explorer — high openness, low conscientiousness, energized by improvisation — Germany can feel like wearing a suit two sizes too small, and the question is whether you're adapting or masking. Adaptation is learning the register: you plan because plans are the local love language, but you still know who you are. Masking is performing conscientiousness sixteen hours a day and quietly concluding your temperament is a defect — that road runs toward burnout and a strange, lonely competence. Two things help. First, this culture hands you a structural gift most don't: Feierabend is institutionalized permission to stop performing — actually use it. Second, the restraint norm means nobody will ask how you're doing, so you have to tell someone; find your Verein, or a therapist — Germans genuinely go, even if the Kassenplatz waiting list tests your newfound long-term orientation.
voiceNotes.skeptic: Quick epistemic check before you treat these deltas as physics. Hofstede's numbers are country means from IBM employee surveys taken fifty years ago; the distributions overlap so much that a random Berliner and a random Bavarian can easily differ more than the German and Dutch averages do. Some of this pack is genuinely well-supported: directness norms, punctuality expectations, and the written-procedure reflex in German institutions are documented across multiple lines of evidence, and you'll observe them within a week. But 'Germans are orderly' as a personality claim? Cross-cultural Big Five studies find national stereotypes barely correlate with measured trait means. So use these scores as priors on public behavior — how the median stranger will react to what you visibly do — and never as a read on the actual person in front of you, who has not taken the survey and does not owe the average anything.

switzerland.overview: Swiss society structurally rewards demonstrated reliability — precision, punctuality, procedural correctness, and long-horizon consistency — and converts those into deep but slowly granted trust. It punishes surprise in most forms: ambush proposals, last-minute cancellations, improvised rule-bending, and visible claims to status, because competition here is intense but conducted quietly through quality of work. Authority is flat and earned; the person who takes the worst volunteer shift often outranks, socially, the person with the biggest title. Newcomers who mistake reserve for rejection, or who try to charm their way past the rules, pay a tax that simple compliance would have waived.
norms: Be five minutes early, and treat every stated plan — a lunch, a deadline, a laundry slot — as a signed contract.
Circulate proposals before the meeting; decisions ripen through prior consultation, and the meeting mostly ratifies what the corridor has already agreed.
Compete through quality, not volume: let your work, your punctuality, and your paperwork brag for you — never your mouth, your salary, or your car.
Follow shared-space rules exactly — quiet hours, recycling, the Waschplan. Neighbors enforce them horizontally, and your compliance is your reputation.
Use the official channel for every conflict: forms, deadlines, arbitration boards. It's free, it works, and filing carries no stigma.
Expect years, not weeks, before you're in. Join a Verein, take the unglamorous volunteer shifts, and let trust accumulate at its own pace.

scenarios.title: The Tolerance Error
scenarios.setup: Three months into your engineering job at a precision-machinery firm in Winterthur, you find a tolerance error in a component spec that has already survived two review rounds. The weekly planning meeting is Monday at 08:00 — and it starts at 08:00. Fixing it would move a delivery date the firm has never once missed.

choices.text: You open Monday's meeting by presenting the flaw, your solution, and a task list — assigning follow-ups to colleagues before anyone else has spoken.
choices.feedback: The room receives it in polite silence, and your team lead reroutes the item to the responsible engineer 'for proper assessment.' The flaw itself is taken seriously — this is a precision firm — but your delivery costs you: proposals here tend to ripen through pre-consultation, and at a power distance this low nobody, including your boss, assigns work by decree. The fix eventually ships with someone else's name on the process.

choices.text: You stay late all week machining a test piece that proves the flaw beyond argument, then present hard measurements with your name on every chart.
choices.feedback: The data lands; measured proof is the one kind of self-assertion this culture reliably respects, and the spec gets corrected. Swiss competitiveness runs on demonstrated quality, so results buy real standing — though a senior colleague dryly notes that leaving at six with the same data would have counted double, since staying late here tends to hint at poor planning rather than heroism.

choices.text: You document the deviation to the third decimal, cite the relevant ISO norm, and hand the dossier to the responsible engineer on Thursday so it can enter Monday's agenda properly.
choices.feedback: The responsible engineer thanks you, the item appears on the agenda with your documentation attached, and the delivery date is renegotiated without drama. Precision routed through the correct procedure is the local love language: a flaw caught and filed properly makes you trustworthy rather than troublesome, and word of the dossier travels further than any speech would have.

choices.text: Over coffee breaks you sound out the two engineers who own the spec, fold their objections into your proposal, and let your team lead table it on Monday.
choices.feedback: By Monday the fix is pre-agreed and passes in four minutes flat. You gave the credit away and bought something better: the spec owners now count you as someone who works correctly — an entry in a ledger this culture keeps for years, not quarters. One of them does hint that for a measurable defect, a written dossier alone would have sufficed; the full choreography is for contested terrain.

scenarios.title: Sunday at Twelve Sharp
scenarios.setup: Sunday lunch at your partner's parents' house in Aargau was fixed three weeks ago: 12:00, Sonntagsbraten, done by 15:30. You wake to a flawless July morning and a text from friends heading to the Seebad for a spontaneous lake day.

choices.text: You call at 10:15 and ask to move lunch to next weekend — the lake only looks like this a few days a year.
choices.feedback: Your partner's mother says 'of course' in a tone that means the opposite, and the story of the cancellation outlives the summer. A fixed plan here is close to a contract: reliability is how this family measures character, and a sunny sky is not force majeure. Your partner spends the drive home not talking about it, which is worse than talking about it.

choices.text: At the table, you warmly press your partner's mother about her recent knee operation and offer to coordinate her physio appointments.
choices.feedback: She answers in two polite sentences and steers the conversation to the weather. Asking after the knee is fine; offering to run her physio calendar is not — in this individualist, reserved culture, managing one's own health is a private domain, and a newer family member volunteering to administer it tends to read as overstep rather than warmth. You will be invited into that room eventually; you cannot knock the door down with kindness.

choices.text: You say little, refill glasses, and ask the father one precise question about the model railway in his basement — referencing a detail he mentioned at Christmas.
choices.feedback: He talks for forty minutes and later tells your partner you are 'vernünftig' — sensible — which is close to a medal. Swiss belonging runs on the long game: remembered details and low-key consistency accumulate trust the way loud charm rarely does, and this family plays by much the same rules as the Verein and the office.

choices.text: You joke, fondly, that this family books its fun three weeks in advance and probably keeps a spreadsheet for spontaneity.
choices.feedback: A beat of silence; then the father says, without smiling, 'Yes. That is why we never miss it.' Enjoyment here is genuinely prized — these people ski, hike, and swim more than you do — but it is protected by structure, and mocking the scaffolding that guarantees the fun wins you nothing at this particular table.

scenarios.title: The Note in the Stairwell
scenarios.setup: A typed, unsigned note appears in the entryway of your Zurich apartment building: someone has been running the washing machine past the 22:00 Nachtruhe and putting cardboard into ordinary Züri-Säcke instead of out for the bundled Karton collection. The Waschplan hangs beside it, and your laundry slot is highlighted in yellow.

choices.text: You reread the Hausordnung, bundle your cardboard with string for Thursday's Karton collection, and from now on finish laundry by 21:45 — no reply, no fuss.
choices.feedback: Within weeks the notes stop, and the pensioner from the second floor starts greeting you by name. Rules about noise, laundry, and recycling are the grammar of shared space in Switzerland; silent, exact compliance is read as respect for the community, and it buys more goodwill than any apology speech could.

choices.text: You pin up a reply: adults should not police each other's laundry hours, and whoever wrote the note is welcome to come say it to your face.
choices.feedback: Nobody comes to your face; instead the Hausverwaltung sends a registered letter citing the Hausordnung, and the stairwell goes cold. You have imported the wrong individualism: the Swiss kind is real but domain-bounded — your salary, your politics, and your weekends are nobody's business, while the stairwell, the Waschküche, and the Nachtruhe sit on the communal side of the fence, where neighbors enforcing shared rules on each other counts as civic virtue, not pettiness.

choices.text: You knock on the Hauswart's door, apologize plainly for the slip, and ask him to walk you through the Waschplan and the recycling calendar.
choices.feedback: He softens visibly, lends you the official Entsorgungskalender, and mentions which neighbor wrote the note — 'she means well.' Going straight to the designated responsible person works in a flat, functional hierarchy: the Hauswart is approachable precisely because his role is defined, and owning the mistake without drama closes the file.

choices.text: You counter the frost with warmth: a handwritten invitation to a Saturday apéro in the courtyard, your treat, so the building can finally meet properly.
choices.feedback: Four neighbors attend, are impeccably polite for fifty minutes, and the following week a fresh note appears — the cardboard was never addressed. The apéro is genuinely enjoyed; it just doesn't touch the ledger that matters. Trust in a Swiss building accrues through years of correct, predictable behavior, and charm gets filed in a separate drawer from your reliability record.

scenarios.title: Clubhouse Rules
scenarios.setup: You've joined a Turnverein in Zurich — the classic route into local life — and after Thursday training the group settles in at the clubhouse over beers. You've just landed a major promotion, with a bonus that still makes you grin. Someone asks, mildly, how work is going.

choices.text: You share the good news properly: the promotion, the ballpark of the number, and a celebratory round for the whole table on you.
choices.feedback: The round is accepted, the subject is changed, and you are never quite asked about work again. Swiss competitiveness is real but worn under a plain jacket: wealth is what you do not mention, and a bought round that announces success reads as showing off rather than generosity. The club will remember the number longer than you will.

choices.text: 'Going fine, thanks' — and you turn the question around, asking the veteran beside you how the club fared at last summer's Kantonalturnfest.
choices.feedback: He tells you, at length, and you learn who actually runs this place. Career and money are private property in this individualist culture, so deflecting the question is not evasive here — it's literate — and curiosity about the club is the currency that actually trades at this table.

choices.text: When the sign-up sheet for the club festival circulates, you take the slot nobody wants: sausage grill, Saturday, setup at 06:00.
choices.feedback: The Präsident himself takes the shift next to yours — he's a cantonal bank executive, and inside the clubhouse that means nothing. Fronarbeit is how Vereinsleben works: at this power distance, status buys no exemption from grunt work, and volunteering for the worst shift unprompted marks you, quietly and durably, as one of them.

choices.text: Three weeks in, you've spotted obvious inefficiencies — you propose a restructured training plan to the committee and offer to run it yourself.
choices.feedback: The committee thanks you and tables it 'for the autumn assembly,' where it will die peacefully. The Verein has run this drill order since before you arrived in the country; in a long-term-oriented culture, the right to change an institution is earned through years of showing up, not weeks of good ideas.

scenarios.title: The Yellow Form
scenarios.setup: Your Zurich landlord sends a formal letter raising your rent, citing 'general cost increases' — but the reference interest rate (Referenzzinssatz) just fell, which normally means rents go down. The official form gives you 30 days to contest the increase at the cantonal Schlichtungsbehörde, the free tenancy arbitration board.

choices.text: You look up the Referenzzinssatz tables, calculate the legally supportable rent, and file the challenge by registered post with your arithmetic attached — well inside the deadline.
choices.feedback: At the hearing, the landlord's agent glances at your numbers and settles before the board even rules; your rent goes down. Contesting through the Schlichtungsbehörde is not aggression here — it is the designed channel, free and routine — and a Swiss counterparty tends to respect nothing more than a deadline met with correct figures.

choices.text: You call the landlord's office for a friendly chat, trusting that a good tenant relationship and a reasonable tone will soften the increase without formal unpleasantness.
choices.feedback: The property manager is perfectly pleasant, promises to 'look into it,' and the 30-day deadline quietly expires — taking your legal right to contest with it. In this rule-based, individualist system, rights live in procedures, not relationships; choosing harmony over the form is read not as gracious but as not having done your homework.

choices.text: You fire back a scorching letter threatening legal consequences and demand the landlord meet you in person within the week.
choices.feedback: You receive a two-line reply referring you to 'the ordinary legal channels' — which were always yours to use for free. Assertiveness here must be sachlich: cold, factual, procedural. Heat is not read as strength but as a loss of form, and you've burned goodwill you may want back at the hearing.

choices.text: You knock on every door in the building, compile who else received the letter, and organize a joint challenge with yourself as the tenants' spokesperson.
choices.feedback: Five households sign on, the Mieterverband helps you file as a bloc, and the board takes the coordinated case seriously. At this power distance, organizing upward against a landlord is unremarkable civic behavior — the militia principle (Milizprinzip) applied to a stairwell — and orderly, form-correct leadership is one of the few kinds this society will actually follow.

caveats: Hofstede's Swiss data is usually split by language region: French-speaking Switzerland scores far higher on power distance and uncertainty avoidance (roughly PDI ~70, UAI ~70 in Hofstede's own regional tables) than the German-speaking majority this profile mostly reflects, and Ticino differs again. A Geneva or Lausanne scenario pack would need different deltas.

The first four scores derive from IBM employee surveys of the late 1960s-70s; LTO 74 and IVR 66 were bolted on decades later from Minkov's World Values Survey reanalysis, so they rest on a different instrument entirely. Meanwhile roughly 40% of residents in cities like Zurich and Geneva have a migration background, and international workplaces (Basel pharma, Geneva NGOs, Zug crypto-finance) often run on Anglo norms where several of these penalties never fire.

Urban, young, and creative-sector Switzerland tolerates spontaneity and status display far more than the median Gemeinde; conversely, a village in Appenzell or Central Switzerland enforces conformity harder than any scenario here. The simulation aims at a big-city middle that many residents don't inhabit.

The game compresses distinct mechanisms — statutory rules (Nachtruhe), private house rules (Hausordnung), and pure custom (Sunday laundry taboos) — into one social score, but real sanctions differ sharply: a registered letter from the Verwaltung is not a cold shoulder in the stairwell. And the classic Waschplan itself is fading — many newer city buildings run free-use laundry rooms or in-unit machines, so the most stereotyped scenario here is also the most dated.

socialDelta scores reflect mainstream norm enforcement, not what is effective or right for any individual: plenty of successful, well-liked people in Zurich violate several of these norms daily and absorb the costs happily.

voiceNotes.archetypist: Switzerland is what happens when a society decides order will be maintained from below rather than imposed from above: PDI 34 combined with UAI 58 means everyone is responsible for the structure and no one is exempt from it. That's aristocracy for the conscientious — the craftsman and the sage hold rank here, because industriousness and orderliness ARE the status hierarchy, just denominated in reliability instead of titles. Notice the entry fee, though: assertiveness must be decoupled from display. The hero who needs an audience starves; the one who can let ten years of flawless work speak quietly inherits the canton. Pick up responsibility nobody assigned you — the laundry roster, the club grill, the tenants' petition — and the hierarchy will find you on its own.
voiceNotes.clinician: If you run high on spontaneity or emotional expressiveness, be honest about what this environment asks: not one performance but a permanent baseline of scheduled, contained living, and chronic masking at that dose is expensive — it surfaces as low-grade resentment, Sunday dread, the sense of being managed by your own calendar. The good news is that Swiss structure is legible: the rules are literally written down, the sanctions are predictable, and IVR 66 means real joy is available — it's just booked in advance. Adaptation can be genuine rather than performative if you find the sanctioned containers for your chaos: the mountains, the lake at 6 a.m., Basel's Fasnacht, where an entire society schedules its own id. But if after two or three years the reserve still feels like rejection and the precision like surveillance, that isn't a character flaw to fix with more effort — it's data about fit, and you're allowed to weigh it.
voiceNotes.skeptic: Real talk on the data: these Hofstede numbers are decades-old survey aggregates — the first four dimensions from IBM offices in the late 1960s-70s, LTO and IVR from a later World Values Survey reanalysis — and Switzerland is a genuinely awkward case because the German- and French-speaking regions score differently enough that one national profile is doing heavy averaging. What's well-supported: punctuality norms, formal-channel dispute resolution, and quiet-money culture are extensively documented, and you'll verify all three within a week of arriving. What to hold loosely: any claim about what 'the Swiss' are like as individuals — country averages explain a small slice of person-level variance, and the spread inside Zurich dwarfs the gap between Zurich and Munich. Treat this pack as a prior on institutions, not a stereotype about people; when you meet a loud, chaotic, spontaneous Swiss person — and you will, constantly — the model didn't break, because it was never about individuals.

usa.overview: Metro America pays out for legible individual achievement: self-authored, quantified, optimistically narrated, and refreshed quarterly. It tends to punish invisible service, unleveraged loyalty, and public negativity — while forgiving failure, job-hopping, and reinvention that would be disqualifying elsewhere. Hierarchy dresses casual but keeps score in money and metrics, and relationships are warm, voluntary, and revocable. The system is genuinely open and genuinely indifferent: nobody will stop you, and nobody will catch you.
norms: Narrate your own wins, with numbers. Modesty tends to read as absence of impact, not as virtue — unclaimed work mostly doesn't count.
Default to upbeat. Vent to one close friend or a therapist; public complaining rarely starts a debate — it tends to get you quietly dropped from the invite list.
Make the ask directly — the raise, the intro, the favor. Directness is respected here, and hints mostly go undecoded.
Treat small talk and networking as sincere social forms, not phoniness. The warmth is real; it's just wide and shallow, and that's the design.
Failure converts to an asset if you frame it as Act One of the comeback. Hidden, it tends to curdle into stigma.
First-name the CEO, joke with your boss — then remember the org chart and the money are still keeping score. Informality is a style, not a truce.

scenarios.title: Brag Doc Season
scenarios.setup: It's perf season at your Series B startup in Austin. Your manager Slacks the team: 'Reminder — brag docs due Friday for calibration.' You spent the quarter doing unglamorous migration work that kept the flagship launch from collapsing, and a louder teammate is already posting launch metrics with rocket-ship emojis.

choices.text: Write a brag doc that claims your migration work in hard numbers — uptime saved, launch unblocked — and post the highlight reel in the team channel before calibration.
choices.feedback: Your manager quotes your numbers verbatim in the calibration meeting and you land an 'exceeds.' In brag-doc culture, self-report tends to be the official data source, and MAS-62 pays for visible, quantified winning — work that isn't written down rarely gets counted.

choices.text: Skip your own doc to help two overwhelmed teammates finish theirs, and quietly clear the on-call backlog nobody wants to touch.
choices.feedback: Calibration lands you at 'meets expectations,' and your manager, genuinely apologetic, says he 'didn't have the data.' Nobody punishes the helping — IDV-91 just attaches credit to named individuals, so glue work is real work that tends to go officially unrecorded. The penalty is omission, not hostility.

choices.text: Submit a strictly accurate doc centered on code health, test coverage, and the maintenance debt you paid down, refusing to inflate anything.
choices.feedback: The review says 'solid, but limited impact this quarter.' Stewardship is a long-term asset in a short-term ledger: LTO-26 tends to score quarters, not decades, so durability often reads as an absence of wins.

choices.text: Reply in the team channel that brag docs are performance theater that rewards writers over builders, and say you won't be submitting one.
choices.feedback: You get three private 'so true' DMs and one public 'feedback is a gift!' from your manager — plus a quiet note about 'attitude.' Contrarianism sells in a job interview; sustained public negativity violates IVR-68's upbeat norm, and persistent complainers tend to get managed around, then out, politely.

scenarios.title: The Sunday Call
scenarios.setup: You're on the Sunday-night phone call with your parents in Ohio. Your dad's knee replacement is scheduled for March, your mom keeps mentioning how nice it is that your cousin 'stayed close to home' — and you have an offer letter from a San Francisco company open on your screen: 40% raise, relocation paid.

choices.text: Take the offer, tell your parents that night, and frame it as the adventure it is — new city, new chapter, flights home for the holidays.
choices.feedback: Your mom cries a little and then says what so many American parents say: 'We'd never want to hold you back.' IDV-91 makes your trajectory the family's official priority; the guilt is real, but the norm is to process it privately — often with a therapist.

choices.text: Turn the offer down and start planning a move back to Ohio to run point on Dad's surgery and recovery yourself.
choices.feedback: Your parents are moved; your peers say 'that's so sweet' with a half-second pause. In an achievement-scored culture, years off the career ladder tend to read as lost rank rather than honored duty — the sacrifice is admired briefly and repriced quietly.

choices.text: Convene a family video call, present a plan — a hired home-health aide for six weeks, a shared care calendar, costs split with your sister — and take the offer.
choices.feedback: Your sister is visibly relieved someone 'owned it,' and your parents accept the plan after negotiating details. In a PDI-40 family, elders are stakeholders rather than authorities: care delivered through logistics and paid professionals is the legitimate individualist compromise, even though it would scan as cold in many family cultures — including plenty inside these same metros.

choices.text: Keep the call pleasant, steer around both the surgery and the offer, and decide nothing until the mood is better.
choices.feedback: Two weeks later your mom asks your sister if you're 'hiding something,' and the offer deadline forces a rushed yes anyway. Direct, low-context talk is the individualist default here — the unsaid tends to be treated as nonexistent, so harmony maintained by avoidance often reads as flakiness rather than consideration.

scenarios.title: The Party House Out Back
scenarios.setup: The house behind yours in East Austin turned into a full-time short-term rental, and every weekend a different bachelorette party's rented Suburban blocks your driveway. The Nextdoor thread about it is at 87 comments, and the neighborhood association meets Thursday.

choices.text: Message the owner through the listing, keep it friendly — 'hey neighbor!' — and suggest he add a bold parking note to his check-in instructions and a cone for your driveway.
choices.feedback: He apologizes within the hour, updates the listing, and drops off a six-pack. IVR-68 runs on cheerful, low-stakes friendliness between strangers; offering an easy, face-saving fix before any authority got involved makes you 'a great neighbor' on the very thread you never posted in.

choices.text: Document every blocked-driveway incident with timestamped photos, then file a 311 report and a formal complaint against his short-term-rental license before speaking to anyone.
choices.feedback: The city opens a case — the procedure genuinely works — but Austin's 311 records are public, the complaint surfaces on Nextdoor, and the vibe curdles toward 'narc.' UAI-46 prefers the improvised handshake fix: going rulebook-first without a friendly attempt tends to read as officious rather than diligent.

choices.text: Post the owner's name and the party-house photos on Nextdoor with a caption about greed destroying the neighborhood.
choices.feedback: You get 62 likes and one 'THANK YOU' — then someone mentions defamation, someone screenshots it to the owner, and two neighbors stop waving. Outrage is engagement online, but IVR-68's optimism norm governs real-world standing: public shaming makes you polarizing rather than heroic, and the moderates now file you under 'the conflict.'

choices.text: Say nothing online, read the city's short-term-rental ordinance over the weekend, and deliver one precise two-minute statement at Thursday's meeting citing the exact code section on licensing.
choices.feedback: The board — three retirees and a realtor — adopts your language for their letter to the city almost word for word. PDI-40 keeps boards and officials approachable: a prepared nobody with the right citation frequently outranks an angry somebody with seniority.

scenarios.title: Run Club Economics
scenarios.setup: Three weeks after the layoff hit your whole team, a former coworker drags you to an Austin run club that is transparently a networking scene — 5K first, then tacos and the 'so, what do you do?' carousel. Your LinkedIn still lists the old company.

choices.text: Answer straight: 'Got caught in the RIF three weeks ago — honestly a reset I needed. I'm looking for staff-level product roles. Who should I be talking to?'
choices.feedback: By the second round of tacos you have two intros and someone's Notion doc of hiring managers. UAI-46 keeps failure cheap: careers are expected to be discontinuous, so a layoff carries little stigma when narrated as Act One of the comeback — and the direct ask tends to be the respected close, provided you name exactly what you want.

choices.text: Hang back, listen to the conversations around the table, and speak only when you can add something genuinely substantive.
choices.feedback: You make two genuinely smart contributions and nobody texts you afterward. In an indulgent, enthusiasm-priced scene, reserve rarely reads as depth — it reads as low energy, and low energy tends not to get remembered, let alone referred.

choices.text: Lean into funemployment: the Baja trip you finally booked, the welding class, the half-formed app idea — high energy, zero agenda.
choices.feedback: You're the most fun person at the table and get added to the group chat by dessert. IVR-68 genuinely rewards whoever brings the fun; the job leads will arrive slower than on the direct-ask path, but you're in the room now, and the room is the asset.

choices.text: Deflect the question each time it reaches you and become the best listener at the table, drawing out the shy guy who just moved from Ohio.
choices.feedback: Everyone finds you lovely, and a week later nobody can say what you do. Nothing bad happens — and nothing happens. 'Tell me about yourself' is the social API of an IDV-91 culture: return no self-narrative and you simply don't get written into anyone's mental rolodex.

scenarios.title: The Counteroffer
scenarios.setup: Eighteen months into your job — already median tenure on your team — a recruiter's process you entered 'just for practice' ends in a written offer: 25% more money, better title. You like your manager, Dana. Your one-on-one with her starts in an hour.

choices.text: Put the offer on the table plainly: you'd rather stay, here's the number, and can she match it within two weeks.
choices.feedback: Dana asks for a day, files a retention request, and comes back at 22% plus a title bump. In an at-will, achievement-scored labor market, comp is a scoreboard and leverage is the legitimate way to move it; few respect you less for playing a game everyone knows is running — though some managers will quietly start succession planning.

choices.text: Don't mention the offer — you don't play games. Ask for a raise strictly on the merits: eighteen months of reliable, documented, high-quality work.
choices.feedback: Dana agrees you deserve more and returns with the standard 4% band adjustment — 'that's what comp will approve without a competing offer.' Tenure and duty aren't currency in an LTO-26 labor market: the system prices market leverage, and unilateral loyalty tends to be a discount you give, not one you're paid for.

choices.text: Skip the offer talk; tell Dana you want the promotion path made explicit, and propose taking ownership of the flailing platform migration to earn it.
choices.feedback: Dana loops in her director that week, and you leave with a written promo plan tied to the migration. PDI-40 makes self-nomination legitimate rather than presumptuous — visibly volunteering for hard, ownable problems is a recognized route up, though without outside leverage the money usually moves slower than the title.

choices.text: Tell Dana the whole truth: you got an offer, you feel guilty even considering it, the team depends on you — what does she think is fair?
choices.feedback: Dana is warm and reassuring in the meeting — and afterward you're likely logged as a flight risk who probably won't fly, which prices you as safe to underpay. MAS-62 hides weakness and assumes negotiation: vulnerability handed up the org chart tends to become data, not intimacy.

caveats: This pack models coastal and Sunbelt metro professional culture (NYC, Austin, Bay Area). Rural and small-town America, the church-anchored South, and the modesty-normed Upper Midwest run meaningfully different payoff tables — several caregiver and craftsman moves penalized here would score positive there.

Provenance is uneven: PDI, IDV, MAS, and UAI descend from IBM employee surveys of 1967-73, while LTO 26 and IVR 68 were bolted on around 2010 from Minkov's World Values Survey reanalysis — different respondents, different decades, different instruments. Later work (GLOBE, WVS) confirms America's individualism rank but not the numbers' precision, and MAS 62 is among the most contested US scores.

Class, race, and gender change the payoffs: the double-bind literature documents that assertiveness and self-promotion are received differently depending on who performs them, which country-level averages cannot see. The +2 hero moves here are least reliable for people the culture stereotypes as 'should be modest.'

Immigrant families — a large share of exactly these metros — often run collectivist family scripts inside individualist workplaces; the family scenario's deltas assume the Anglo-American mainstream and will misprice many real households.

Institutional variance persists even among the named metros: at-will employment and HR culture are near-universal (Montana excepted on at-will), but HOA power, Nextdoor intensity, tech-labor leverage, and networking density differ sharply between NYC, Austin, and the Bay.

voiceNotes.archetypist: This is the highest individualism score Hofstede ever recorded, and its low power distance means no hierarchy will claim you — you have to climb voluntarily, visibly, and out loud. The trait data are unambiguous about what the system pays: assertiveness plus industriousness, the hero and sovereign patterns, with the ladder rebuilt every quarter because a short-term-oriented culture lets yesterday's competence buy you almost nothing. The bargain is at least honest. Pick up something heavy in public — a project, a problem, a room — and state plainly that you're carrying it; order here isn't handed down from above, it's assembled by whoever accepts responsibility first, and that assembly keeps getting rewarded.
voiceNotes.clinician: If your temperament runs reserved, agreeable, or high in negative emotion, notice what this place is actually asking of you: a chronic performance of enthusiasm and self-advocacy, which is a form of masking, and masking carries a real metabolic cost — part of why burnout here so often presents as 'I don't even know who I am at work anymore.' The optimism norm creates a strange paradox: it is high-status to have a therapist and low-status to be visibly struggling, so distress goes underground until it becomes a crisis. Adaptation is fine — learn the brag doc, learn the ask — but keep two or three relationships where the mask comes fully off, and treat those as infrastructure, not indulgence. The goal is not to become the hero archetype; it's to rent the behavior for an hour and then come back to your own side.
voiceNotes.skeptic: Let's separate what's supported from what's vibes. Self-promotion, direct negotiation, and networking paying off in US professional settings — reasonably solid, act on it. Much of the rest rests on a fifty-year-old IBM survey (with the last two dimensions bolted on from World Values Survey data decades later) plus pattern-matching, and the honest statistical point is that within-country variance dwarfs these between-country averages: a reserved engineer in Columbus and an Austin sales rep differ more from each other than the average American differs from the average Japanese. So treat every delta in this pack as a weak prior about the room, not a law about the person in front of you — they didn't take the survey, and they will surprise you.
